t1.verdict: Partially supported. Worth building for the sparse regime (x70) only, once the mechanism is corrected. The idea itself is not new. The SSD restore really is exposed: 19-20% of x70 returning turns are restored from SSD, at 2.8-3.3 s p50 TTFT against 0.25 s for host hits. The next turn is near-certain (97%), and gaps of at least 47 s leave plenty of lead time, so in simulation a pre-arrival fetch hides 81-100% of the read. But most of the exposed time is queueing behind other SSD reads, which are issued reactively, served one at a time and arrive in bursts. It is not mainly a shallow queue failing to hide a single read. The lead has to cover the L3 backlog (about 10-20 s here), and it must stay below L2 survival time (roughly 20-30 s at peak) unless the fetched pages are protected. The replays cannot show that gaps are predictable: history-based predictors keep only 54-71% of the benefit, and an over-estimate of 25% or more keeps none.
what_is_right: Tier resolution is tied to arrival. _add_request_to_queue calls self._prefetch_kvcache(req) and then waiting_queue.append(req) (scheduler.py:3148-3155). prefetch_start matches ReqTimeStats entry_time within 1-2 ms (n=4,659/4,660, x1 SSD arms).

The SSD fetch is on the critical path. wait_complete skips the request until its fetch ends (scheduler.py:3817-3821). L3 insert to admission is p50 0.00 s at x70. Storage-hit TTFT p50 is 2.76 s (to) / 3.34 s (wc), against 0.25 / 0.24 s for host hits.

The private context is reused. 4,548 of 4,676 replies (97.3%) are followed by another turn. Storage hits restore about 20.3-20.5K tokens of prompts around 29K, so fetching a session's last context is wasted only on final turns (about 3%).
There is lead time. Every x70 L3-hit gap is at least 46.9 s (to) / 47.9 s (wc), p50 52 / 84 s. A turn's own read takes about 0.8-0.9 s, and even congested fetch windows stay at or below 20-22 s.

Starting before arrival works when timed against the true arrival. In a single-reader EDF simulation (validated, median io_end error -0.029 s), a 10 s lead hides 81-91% of fetch time and a 20 s lead about 100%. Storage-hit TTFT mean falls 5.18 -> 1.27 s (to) and 5.57 -> 0.32 s (wc).
The SSD has spare bandwidth to shift reads into. The read thread is busy 23-27% of the read span (73-77% idle), but 85-89% during the +1200-1500 s burst.
what_is_wrong_or_imprecise: Mechanism. A shallow queue is not the main cause. Storage hits that arrive to an empty queue (37-39% of hits) expose only about 0.7 s each and carry 5-7% of fetch-window time. Hits arriving at queue depth >=5 carry 72-81% of it, and that queue is mostly other requests waiting for L3: corr(queue depth, pending reads) = 0.85 / 0.99. Waiting on the single L3 read thread (cache_controller.py:447-448, 1136-1141) is 58% (to) / 80% (wc) of storage-hit TTFT. In bursts, 10-s offered read demand reaches about 2.1x the SSD bandwidth.

The queue-entry 'prefetch' is only an L3->L2 fetch. It covers only the suffix that L1+L2 miss, and only if that suffix is at least 256 tokens (unified_radix_cache.py:1759-1769). The L2->L1 load happens at admission (schedule_policy.py:1305-1316).

Timing. 'Estimated tool return minus fetch time' gives too short a lead. Moving each fetch earlier by only its own read time (size / bandwidth) hides just 16-24%, because early restores still collide with each other. The lead must include the predicted L3 backlog (10-20 s here), and reads must be served in order of predicted deadline (EDF), not FIFO.

'Even earlier' has an upper limit. Fetched pages are inserted unlocked (unified_radix_cache.py:2024). Fetching at the end of the reply re-evicts 77% of fetched contexts (net 13-19% of fetch time hidden) and parks an average of 37% of L2. Without protection, leads of 30 s / 60 s re-evict 20-25% / 56-64%.

Gap predictability is assumed, not shown. The replay gaps are deterministic trace gaps x70, and 37% of them fall in 49-53 s. History predictors land within ±25% for only 34-50% of L3-hit turns, and they are biased low, because the turns that fall to L3 are the ones with long gaps. Any over-estimate of 25% or more loses the whole benefit. Tool-call-based prediction is not tested by this data. Ask the Tool reports about 80% median error for history predictors.

The queueing-delay estimate must be server-side. The replay client's default aiohttp 100-connection cap (replay_agentic.py:265) adds lag that the server never sees: p50 0.07 s at x70, but 2-7 s at x10/x1 (p95 42-51 s).
Scope. This applies to the sparse regime only. At x10/x1, storage hits are 0.1-0.2% of turns, and queue waits of about 100 s would hide any read.

Part of the SSD residency that T1 targets comes from inclusion. About 40% of L2 mirrors L1. A session-level LRU model predicts that reclaiming that mirror would cut x70 SSD/cold returns from 21% to 2.7-4.5%, which would shrink T1's opportunity.
t1.corrected_statement: In the sparse regime (x70), about one returning turn in five (19.7% / 18.6%) finds its private context only on SSD. HiCache resolves tiers only when the request reaches the scheduler, so each SSD restore starts at arrival, and a single read thread serves restores in FIFO order. Restores arrive in bursts: 10-s offered demand reaches about 2.1x the 1.88 GiB/s SSD, even though the SSD is about 75% idle overall. A typical restore therefore waits 3.0-4.4 s behind other restores, plus about 0.85 s for its own read. Storage-hit TTFT is 2.8-3.3 s p50 (5.2-5.6 s mean), against 0.25 s for host hits. A session's next turn is near-certain (97%) and follows a gap of at least about 47 s, so the restore can start before the turn arrives, under three conditions. (a) Reads are served earliest predicted arrival first. (b) The lead covers the read plus the predicted L3 backlog: about 10-20 s here, not the roughly 1 s read time. (c) The fetched pages are protected in L2 until used, or the lead is kept short enough to survive L2 turnover; without protection, leads beyond about 30 s are mostly re-evicted. Timed against the true arrivals, this hides 81-100% of the fetch and cuts mean returning TTFT by 40-66%. With realistic gap predictors it keeps roughly 54-88% of that gain. An over-estimate of 25% or more falls back to today's behaviour. These replays do not test whether the tool-call type predicts return time well enough.
supporting_numbers: Arrival-bound trigger: |prefetch_start - ReqTimeStats entry_time| p50 1 ms, max 1-2 ms, n=4,659/4,660 (x1 SSD arms, detail.py). Client send -> prefetch_start p50 69 ms at x70 (t1_a.py).

Exposure at x70: 896/4,548 (19.7%, to) and 837/4,509 (18.6%, wc) returns restored from SSD (cached_details.storage>0). Storage-hit TTFT mean 5.18 / 5.57 s, p50 2.76 / 3.34 s, p90 14.48 / 15.06 s, against host-hit p50 0.25 / 0.24 s (t1_b.py).
Excess over host hits in the same 4K prompt bin: 3.52 s (68% of storage-hit TTFT, to) and 5.26 s (95%, wc). Also matched on queue depth: 1.90 s (37%) / 4.25 s (93%) (t1_d.py).

Mean storage-hit TTFT decomposition, to / wc: send->query 0.17 / 0.09 s + waiting for the single L3 read thread 3.01 / 4.43 s + own IO 0.90 / 0.82 s + IO end->admission 0.58 / 0.03 s + admission->first token 0.52 / 0.20 s = 5.18 / 5.57 s (t1_d.py).

Shallow-queue case: 330 (37%) / 325 (39%) of storage hits arrive at queue depth 0, expose about 0.7 s, and carry 7.0% / 5.1% of fetch-window time. The 298 / 307 hits arriving at depth >=5 carry 71.6% / 80.7%, with mean windows of 6.3-14.6 s. corr(queue depth, pending L3 reads) = 0.85 / 0.99 (t1_q.py).

Serialization and bursts: s2h_io intervals overlap 4/960 (to) and 0/837 (wc). Read thread busy 23-27% over the read span, 85.5-88.8% in +1200-1500 s. Offered demand in 10-s windows peaks at 4.09 / 3.94 GiB/s. Per-read throughput p50 1.93 GiB/s, about the SSD ceiling (t1_c.py, t1_bw.py, t1_ts.py).

Lead-time counterfactual (single-reader EDF on true arrivals). Lead = own read time: 24.0% / 16.4% hidden. 5 s: 66.6% / 54.0%. 10 s: 90.8% / 81.0% (storage-hit TTFT mean 1.63 / 1.32 s). 20 s: 100% / 99.9% (1.27 / 0.32 s; the contention-free counterfactual gives 1.11 / 0.23 s). Mean returning TTFT 1.94 -> 1.17 s (-40%, to) and 1.48 -> 0.50 s (-66%, wc) (t1_sim.py, t1_lead.py, t1_e.py, t1_misc.py).

Fetching too early (applies the run's observed L2 survival curve): re-eviction 0.8-1.2% at a 10 s lead, 4.9-7.3% at 20 s, 20-25% at 30 s, 56-64% at 60 s. Fetching at end of reply: 77% re-evicted, net 13-19% hidden, parked contexts average 37% of L2 with a peak of 100-106%. At 10-20 s leads, 5-14% of L2 is parked on average, peak 27% (t1_evict.py, t1_park.py, t1_net.py).

Prediction error: over-estimates of +25% / +50% hide only 0.6-1.3%. Under-estimate of -25% with a 2 s margin: net 85-88%. -50%: net 55-63%. Session-history predictors are within ±25% for 34-50% of L3-hit turns, and the running median under-predicts 98.8-99.0% of them (median error -32% / -43%). Their net is 54-71%, plus 500-700 GiB of extra SSD reads against 1,810 / 1,571 GiB actually read (t1_pred.py, t1_net.py).
Timeout waste (to arm): 64 reads (98 GiB) aborted after a mean 7.42 s wait for the read thread. Those turns recomputed, with mean TTFT 10.41 s (t1_misc.py).
Regime scope: storage hits are 0.1-0.2% at x10/x1. L3 query hits of >=256 tokens: 68/4,538 (x10 to) and 15/4,548 (x1 to), against 960/4,548 at x70 (arrival_loss.py).

closest_prior_work: TokenCake (arXiv 2510.18586; EuroSys '27). A per-tool EWMA predicts function-call completion and drives a gradual CPU->GPU upload 'as the predicted completion time approaches'. It names the too-late vs too-early tension. GPU/CPU only, no queue-wait term, and the released code is still demand-triggered.

Ask the Tool, Don't Guess (arXiv 2609.18849, Sep 2026). Refreshes a context from DRAM 'one lead time before the predicted return', on SWE-agent replays. Shows history predictors are about 80% off and cost 8-13x the reload volume. HBM/DRAM only; the lead is the recovery time, with no queue term.

SYMPHONY (arXiv 2412.16434). Advisory requests carrying expected_arrival let the node manager move a session's KV to the fastest tier before the real request. Prefetched copies may be purged under memory pressure. No timing rule and no queue term.

Announced but not built: NVIDIA Dynamo agentic blog (Apr 2026, storage->GPU 'prefetch hooks' driven by predicted tool return); SGLang RFC #27574 (Prefetch is a TODO) and #36224 (pre-arrival transfer is a non-goal); vLLM AgentX and llm-d blogs (future work).
Pre-arrival prefetch keyed on workflow step, CPU->GPU: KVFlow (NeurIPS'25, built on SGLang), SAGA (arXiv 2605.00528, prefetch at tool start), PBKV (arXiv 2605.06472).
Same signals, different action: Continuum (arXiv 2511.02230) combines a per-tool duration CDF with a sliding-window queueing-delay estimate, but uses them to set a GPU retention TTL.
The queue-entry SSD->host prefetch that T1 criticizes (the baseline): CachedAttention (ATC'24), Strata (arXiv 2508.18572), LMCache (arXiv 2510.09665), SGLang HiCache.

Alternative remedy and counter-evidence. Cake (arXiv 2410.03065) overlaps load with compute instead of starting the load earlier. arXiv 2609.16215 finds speculative prefetch does not pay on a contended link, even with an oracle.

t2.verdict: Partially supported. The symptom is real and is the largest prize in the data. At x10/x1, 93-95% of all prefill recomputes context that was in L1+L2 when the request arrived and on SSD the whole time. That clearly motivates a redesign, but the stated mechanism is mostly wrong. The dominant loss involves no prefetch: the context matched in L1/L2 at arrival is evicted while the request waits. Three things combine. (1) LRU plus the refresh at arrival makes eviction follow FCFS order, so the queue head goes first. (2) The pressure comes from write-through of other requests' prefill completions, which are mostly recomputes themselves (a self-reinforcing loop). (3) Admission re-checks only L1/L2, so the context is never re-fetched. Prefetched pages evicted before use are only 0.4-1.9% of lost tokens. Writes happen mainly at end of prefill, not at request end. The host/HBM 'lock' coupling is structural inclusion: about 40% of L2 mirrors L1. 'Start the prefetch later' has to become: re-resolve against L3 before admission, protect the result until admission, and evict in order of predicted admission. The core idea is published (CachedAttention, ATC'24), and a reactive admission-time re-query is already merged upstream (SGLang #39283/#40042).
what_is_right: Write-through is eager and complete. write_through_threshold = 1 (unified_radix_cache.py:465-467). Every host-written page is also written to SSD 1:1: d2h tokens = h2s tokens in all 6 SSD runs, with 0 L3 cleanups. So every context later lost from L2 was still on SSD (inferred from the aggregates; not checked per rid).
Content found or fetched long before processing gets lost before use. At x1 the loss rate is 0% for server waits under 10 s, 29-35% at 20-30 s, and >=94% beyond 60 s. The median server wait is 111 s.

The literal case does occur in the class that ran. Prefetched pages are inserted and unlocked as soon as the read completes (unified_radix_cache.py:2562-2566, 1983, 2024). At x10/x1, 80-87% of real L3 reads were evicted again before admission (58/68, 57/66, 12/15, 13/15), and each lost its whole span.
Host eviction is forced by other requests' write-through. At x10, 6,667 of 6,723 evict_host events (52.3M of 53.4M tokens) sit next to a d2h_submit; prefetch staging accounts for only 1.08M tokens.
Recomputation follows. 49-55% of returning turns are admitted with only the 7,808-token shared prompt, and these recomputes are 93-95% of all prefill.
Moving the fetch toward processing time is feasible. Re-reading each admitted context just in time needs about 0.6-0.7 GiB/s (32-37% of the SSD) at x1's admission rate.

The host/HBM coupling is a real capacity loss. About 40% of L2 (636-656K tokens) holds copies of device-resident KV in every run, and host eviction began exactly when cumulative write-through reached the size of L2.
what_is_wrong_or_imprecise: Write timing: it is not 'right after the request is done'. 72-98% of host and SSD write volume is written when the last prefill chunk completes (cache_unfinished_req with chunked=False, batch_result_processor.py:353-359), before the first token. Only the decode pages and the page straddling the prompt boundary are written at finish. Intermediate chunks are never backed up (chunked=True). Each SSD write is chained to its host-write ack, with p50 lag 0.02 s at x70 and 0.28-0.34 s at x10/x1.

The dominant loss is not a prefetch. At arrival the history is almost always still in L1+L2 (98.4-99.6% of returns), so no L3 fetch is issued: an L3 query hits >=256 tokens for only 68/4,538 (x10) and 15/4,548 (x1) returns. Prefetched-then-evicted content is 0.4-1.9% of lost tokens; 98-99.6% of lost tokens belong to turns with no L3 load.

Missing cause 1: nothing protects the match while the request waits. The only protection is the prefetch anchor host lock. It is never taken when the unmatched tail is under 256 tokens. It is dropped within milliseconds when L3 holds fewer than 256 matching tokens (prefetch_start->s2h_query p50 1 ms). After a successful fetch it is dropped at insert.

Missing cause 2: the eviction order is the worst possible one. The arrival-time match refreshes last_access_time (unified_tree_core.py:836-839), and host eviction pops the oldest node (evict_policy.py:17-18). So eviction follows FCFS order, and the queue head, which is admitted next, goes first. The queued working set (0.9-1.8M private tokens) is larger than the host-only part of L2 (at most 0.96M).

Missing cause 3: nothing re-checks L3 at admission. Admission re-matches only L1/L2; check_prefetch_progress returns True when there is no ongoing prefetch. The paced retry is off (poll interval 0). Even when enabled, it counts scheduling passes and allows at most 4 attempts, so it is not tied to admission (memory.py:169-183, scheduler.py:3118-3146). Upstream's admission-time re-query is absent from this fork (grep count 0). As a result the SSD tier adds nothing: 54-60% of admissions have only the shared prompt at x10/x1, with or without SSD.

'Newly finished requests' should read 'other requests' prefill completions'. These are 98% of write volume at x10/x1, and most are recomputed prompts. x10/x1 write 54-58M tokens against 5.3M at x70, which is the self-reinforcing loop.

'Lock status' is the wrong mechanism. lock_ref and host_lock_ref are separate counters. What pins host copies is _is_host_leaf (unified_tree_core.py:1889): it rejects any node whose device copy still exists, locked or idle, so under write_through L2 always contains L1. Duplicates are reclaimed only under write_back (unified_tree_core.py:1497), which pays a synchronous D2H on eviction, about 50x the per-token cost of a demote.

The mirror is about 40% of L2 in every regime. The part that is idle and cheap to reclaim is 28.7-30.6% of L2 in the x70 SSD arms, but only 3-6.7% at x10/x1. One data agent estimated 15-18% for x70 hbm_host, but that model assumed running requests' prompts are not backed up, which the prefill-end write evidence contradicts.

The remedy is incomplete. 'Start the prefetch later' cannot help the dominant case, because there is no prefetch to delay. It needs three things: re-resolve against L3 near admission, protect what is found or fetched until admission, and evict in order of predicted admission. Pinning every queued prefix is infeasible (about 1.59M tokens, roughly all of L2).
The queue-delay input must be server-side. 19.9 s of the 131.2 s mean x1 TTFT is client-side lag from the connection cap, which the server never sees.
t2.corrected_statement: Under dense load (x10/x1), write-through backs up each new prompt to host when its prefill completes (72-98% of all write volume) and the decode tail at finish. Every page is then chained to SSD, so the SSD holds every context. A returning turn nearly always still finds its whole previous context in L1+L2 when it reaches the server (98.4-99.6%). So no SSD prefetch is issued, and nothing protects that match while the request waits (median 111 s at x1). Host eviction, forced by other requests' write-through (mostly recomputed prompts), removes the oldest host leaves first. Because the arrival-time match refreshed their LRU stamps, eviction follows FCFS order, and the queue head, next to be admitted, goes first. Admission re-matches only L1/L2 and never asks the SSD again. As a result, 49-55% of returning turns recompute everything except the 7,808-token shared prompt. That is 93-95% of all prefill, and it feeds more write-through and longer queues, a self-reinforcing loop. Prefetched content evicted before admission is a minor special case (0.4-1.9% of lost tokens). The fix is to resolve tiers relative to admission, not arrival: re-resolve against the SSD shortly before predicted admission (from queue position and admission rate), protect what is found or fetched until admission, and evict in order of predicted admission (queue tail first). Pinning the whole queue is infeasible (about 1.59M tokens, all of L2). Separately, the host/HBM coupling is inclusion, not locking. A host copy can be evicted only after its device copy is gone, so about 40% of L2 mirrors L1 in every run. That is a capacity lever independent of timing.
supporting_numbers: Write timing: share of host+SSD write volume written at end of prefill is 81.1% / 72.5% / 97.5% (x70 to / wc / hbm_host), 98.1-98.2% (x10) and 98.3% (x1). Predicted vs logged d2h agree within 0.03% in all 9 runs. On isolated x70 turns, 24,640 tokens were written at prefill end (= expected), 16,064 at finish, 0 during decode (split.py, wt_timing.py).

SSD holds everything: d2h tokens = h2s tokens exactly (53,918,976 x10 to; 57,967,168 x1 to; all 6 SSD runs). 0 'NIXL L3 cleanup' lines and 0 evict_host with tokens<requested. h2s lag p50 0.02 s (x70), 0.28-0.34 s (x10/x1).

Present at arrival: the whole previous context was in L1+L2 for 98.4% (x10) / 99.6% (x1) of returns. Arrival match / prompt p50 0.99 vs admitted cached / prompt p50 0.35-0.37. Median arrival match 23.2-23.4K tokens vs cached at admission 7,808. Arrival match = P - 1 - prefetch_start.tokens.

Lost by admission: full loss (only 7,808 tokens cached) in 49.1-49.3% (x10) and 54.7-54.9% (x1) of returning turns. >=1K tokens lost in 54.6% (x10 to) and 60.0% (x1 to). Lost tokens 49.4-50.3M of 52.9-53.2M prefilled (x10) and 54.1-54.4M of 56.9-57.3M (x1), i.e. 93-95% of all prefill.

Not a prefetch: 98.1% (x10 to) and 99.6% (x1 to) of lost tokens are in turns with no L3 load. The literal case: real L3 reads lost 58/68 and 57/66 (x10), 12/15 and 13/15 (x1), i.e. 0.91-0.94M and 0.21M tokens, or 0.4-1.9% of lost tokens.

Unprotected: tail <256 tokens means no lock (1,167 lost turns at x10 to, 1,309 at x1 to). An L3 miss releases the lock at the next drain, with prefetch_start->s2h_query p50 1 ms, p99 3-10 ms (1,252 / 1,408 lost turns). Fetched pages are unlocked at insert (unified_radix_cache.py:2024).

Dependence on wait (x1, ReqTimeStats queue_duration): lost share is 0% under 10 s, 1.5-1.8% at 10-20 s, 29-35% at 20-30 s, 75-77% at 30-45 s, 84-90% at 45-60 s, 94-95% at 60-75 s, 99.9% at >=150 s. Server wait p10/p50/p90 = 6.7 / 111 / 255 s. By host tokens evicted during the wait: <100K gives 1% lost, 500-750K gives 96%, >=750K gives 99-100%.

Eviction pressure: steady host eviction 6.6-7.3K tok/s (whole-pool turnover about 223 s; host-only share about 131 s). L3 loads are 1.08M tokens against 53.37M evicted (x10 to). Total writes are 54-58M tokens at x10/x1 vs 5.3M at x70.
Queued working set (x1 to): private context of queued requests is 0.91M tokens at minute 18 and 1.71-1.80M at minutes 82-98, against host-only L2 of at most 0.96M and all of L2 at 1.63M.

The SSD tier adds nothing under dense load. Admissions with only the shared prompt cached: x10 53.4% (hbm_host) vs 54.4 / 54.5% (SSD arms); x1 58.7% vs 59.3 / 59.5%. At x70: 37.8% vs 1.4 / 0.0% (allarms.py).

Inclusion: the host copy of device-resident KV averages 636,347-656,346 tokens = 39.1-40.3% of L2 in all 9 runs (mirror.py; the host balance peaks at exactly 1,627,648). The idle, unlocked part (lower bound, mirror minus in-use device KV) is 28.7-30.6% of L2 in the x70 SSD arms, 13.5% in x70 hbm_host, 5.9-6.7% at x10, 3.0% at x1. The first host eviction came when cumulative write-through reached 1,627,584 of 1,627,648 tokens.
Cost of the write_back alternative: demote 0.052-0.058 µs/token vs D2H 2.63-2.66 µs/token (about 50x). A synchronous-D2H counterfactual at x10 costs about 186 s vs 3.7 s measured.

Feasibility: just-in-time reload at x1 ≈ 0.362 admissions/s × 20.6K tokens ≈ 7.5K tok/s ≈ 0.69 GiB/s (37% of the SSD). A second estimate, 54.4M tokens / 8,300 s, gives 32%. Pinning the whole queue ≈ 65 × 24.4K ≈ 1.59M tokens ≈ all of L2.

Client lag: t_send -> server entry p50 2.1-2.4 s (x10) and 7.3 s (x1), p95 42-51 s. x1 mean TTFT 131.2 s = 19.9 s on the client side + 109.4 s server queue + 1.9 s. Cause: aiohttp's default 100-connection limit (replay_agentic.py:265).

Existing knob: hicache_storage_prefetch_retry_poll_interval defaults to 0, meaning off (memory.py:169-179). It is counted in scheduling passes, with at most 4 attempts (memory.py:180-183; scheduler.py:3118-3146).

closest_prior_work: CachedAttention/AttentionStore (USENIX ATC'24). Fetches from disk to host only for a look-ahead window of Lpw = Cmem/Skv queued jobs, and exempts jobs in a longer look-ahead eviction window from eviction, evicting from the tail first. This is T2's core idea, but counted in jobs rather than time, with whole-session items, no in-gap sessions and no write-through interaction.

SGLang upstream #39283/#40042 (merged Sep 2026). _prefetch_after_device_hit_loss re-issues the L3 lookup at admission when the device+host match has shrunk since arrival, and skips the request meanwhile. It is reactive: the fetch latency stays on the critical path. #40011 names 'the device match evicts while the request is queued'. #31887 (unmerged) proposes waiting-queue retries, admission deadlines and an isolated staging partition. #32724 notes that staging finalisation is tied to the FCFS scan.

py-kvcache (arXiv 2609.11744) with vLLM #49902/#50014. Disk->CPU promotions for queued requests are evicted before use and the request recomputes. The remedy is a bounded lookahead plus protection of promotions not yet read.
PCR (arXiv 2603.23049). SSD->DRAM prefetch for a fixed 4-request window of the waiting queue, plus a look-ahead LRU that protects chunks pending requests need.
LMCache vLLM adapter and vLLM v1 connector. The external lookup happens only at the admission scan (the 'late' extreme), and looked-up KV is pinned until the request is scheduled.

Continuum (arXiv 2511.02230) uses a tool-duration CDF plus queueing delay, the same inputs T1/T2 propose, but for a GPU retention TTL, not fetch timing. Adaptive KV Retention (arXiv 2608.30830) sets load-indexed host residency via Little's law.

Classic theory: Cao et al., SIGMETRICS'95 (Do No Harm; a prefetch reserves its slot early). Patterson et al., TIP, SOSP'95 (prefetch horizon). Kimbrel et al., OSDI'96 (fixed horizon / forestall: one just-in-time rule that turns aggressive under backlog).
For the inclusion sub-point: SGLang's own write_back policy (_reclaim_full_host_duplicates, unified_tree_core.py:1497-1556) is the existing non-inclusive design.

unified_design:
Admission-anchored staging (AAS). Every tier decision for a session's next turn is driven by one quantity: its predicted admission time Â, the time the scheduler will actually start its prefill. Today these decisions are driven by the request's arrival time.

1. State
- A session registry, keyed by session id, holds for each live session s:
  - a handle to the radix path committed by its last turn (last node or page-hash chain, n_s tokens, and which pages are in L1, L2 or L3);
  - its status: in-gap, queued or running;
  - Â_s.
- The registry is filled at cache_finished_req (turn end, time t_e). It is updated on arrival and on every scheduling pass.

2. Predicting Â
- In-gap session: Â_s = t_e + Ĝ_q + Ŵ.
  - Ĝ_q is a low quantile (q ≈ 0.1-0.25) of the return-time distribution for this tool type, or a harness hint or live progress when one is available.
  - Ŵ is the predicted server-side wait: requests ahead / μ̂, where μ̂ is the EWMA admission rate.
- Queued at FCFS position p: Â_s = now + p/μ̂, refined by the expected completions of the running batch.
- While a tool is overdue, Â is re-estimated from the residual gap distribution. On arrival, Ĝ is replaced by the true arrival time.
- Only the server-side wait counts. The client's 100-connection cap must be removed first.

3. Timing rule
- Issue the L3→L2 read for s's pages that are not in L1/L2 at S_s = Â_s − (n_s^L3 · 98,304 B / BW + Backlog_EDF(Â_s)/BW + m).
  - BW is the measured SSD read bandwidth.
  - Backlog_EDF is the bytes of pending reads with an earlier Â.
  - m ≈ 2 s is a safety margin.
- The read never starts earlier than Â_s − H, where H is the park horizon.
- Reads are served earliest-Â first (EDF), not FIFO. They run as low-priority traffic that yields to demand reads, and reads plus write-through are paced to stay under BW.
- The same rule covers both regimes with no mode switch:
  - Sparse (Ŵ ≈ 0): the read starts before arrival, with a lead of about 10-20 s at x70 (Takeaway 1).
  - Dense (Ŵ ≫ H): the read starts after arrival, once the request is within p ≤ μ̂ · (read + backlog + m) ≈ 1-2 positions of the head at x1 (Takeaway 2).

4. Residency and protection rule
- For every s with Â_s − now ≤ H, protect both its arrival-time L1/L2 match and any pages staged for it.
  - Protection runs from the moment they are matched or land until admission, when the device lock takes over.
  - Today this match is unprotected when the tail is under 256 tokens, protected for only milliseconds after an L3 miss, and unprotected after insert.
- Use a soft host priority class, not host_lock_ref. Hard locks can make write-through backups skip (unified_radix_cache.py:1412-1414).
- Budget: the sum of n_s over protected sessions must be ≤ β · (L2 − L1 mirror − write-through reserve). If it is over, shrink H so only the earliest-Â sessions stay protected. This is a CachedAttention-style window measured in seconds.
- Little's law sizes it at about μ̂ · H · n̄:
  - x1: 0.362/s × 10 s × 20.6K ≈ 75K tokens ≈ 5% of L2.
  - x70 with a 10-20 s lead: 5-14% of L2 on average, 27% at peak.

5. Eviction order
- Among unprotected host leaves, evict the latest predicted admission first: the queue tail and sessions with long predicted gaps.
- Use LRU only for content that has no session prediction.
- This replaces the arrival-time LRU refresh, which today makes eviction order equal FCFS order and evicts the queue head first.
- Do No Harm: staging for s may only evict content whose Â is later than Â_s.

6. Fallback at admission
- When the FCFS scan reaches s, re-match L1/L2.
- If the match is shorter than the registry expects, re-query L3 with the semantics of upstream _prefetch_after_device_hit_loss.
  - Skip s while the read runs, under a deadline.
  - Choose load or recompute by cost: backlog + read time vs prefill time at current throughput.
- If s arrives before S_s (the gap was over-predicted), start the fetch at arrival. The worst case is therefore today's behaviour.
- If Â slips beyond H, drop protection and re-arm the fetch if the pages are later evicted. A final turn (2.7% of replies) releases immediately.

7. Feedback
- Per regime, measure lateness (fetch finished after admission) and pollution (staged or protected bytes evicted or unused).
- Adapt q, m, H and β from these, as in feedback-directed prefetching (FDP).

8. Optional capacity lever (ablated separately)
- Under host pressure, reclaim the L2 mirrors of idle device-resident nodes whose SSD write has been acked.
- When such a node is later evicted from the device, demote it straight to L3-only, since the SSD already holds every page. If Â is near, re-copy it asynchronously instead.
- This gives non-inclusive L1/L2 without write_back's synchronous D2H.

Signals it needs
- Session id.
- Turn-end event with tool-call type and arguments, plus an optional declared-duration hint or live progress.
- Per-tool gap quantiles, learned online.
- FCFS queue position, EWMA admission rate, and completion estimates for the running batch.
- L3 read backlog in bytes, and measured SSD read and write bandwidth.
- L2 occupancy, mirror size, host eviction rate and protected-budget use.
- A per-session residency map (which pages are in L1, L2, L3).

Hooks in the fork
- Registry: at cache_finished_req.
- Controller: polled from check_hicache_events (scheduler.py:3686).
- Protection: keep fetched pages protected past insert (unified_radix_cache.py:2024), and cover sub-256 tails and L3 misses (1759-1769, 2533).
- Eviction key: evict_policy.py:17-18 and full_component.py:243-253.
- EDF reads: in the prefetch IO thread (cache_controller.py:1136-1141).
- Admission re-check: beside check_prefetch_progress (scheduler.py:3817-3821).
novelty_position:
Neither takeaway is new as an idea, and a paper should claim neither.

Takeaway 1 (early restore): already published or announced.
- Restoring before the turn arrives, timed by a predicted tool return, is published for DRAM→HBM:
  - TokenCake (EuroSys '27);
  - Ask the Tool (arXiv 2609.18849);
  - SYMPHONY's expected_arrival advisories;
  - KVFlow, SAGA and PBKV, which key on workflow steps rather than time.
- For storage it is announced but not built: NVIDIA Dynamo's prefetch hooks, SGLang RFC #27574 (Prefetch is a TODO), and the vLLM and llm-d roadmaps.

Takeaway 2 (late restore and protection): already published, and partly merged upstream.
- Disk→host prefetch bound to queue position, plus eviction exemption for queued work, is CachedAttention (ATC '24). PCR and py-kvcache / vLLM #50014 are recent variants.
- SGLang upstream has merged a reactive admission-time L3 re-query (#39283/#40042). PR #40011 already names queue-time eviction.

The combined rule and its inputs: also prior art.
- A single just-in-time rule that fetches aggressively under backlog and late otherwise is Kimbrel et al.'s forestall (OSDI '96). TIP's prefetch horizon and Cao et al.'s Do-No-Harm give the theory.
- Continuum already combines a tool-duration CDF with a queueing-delay estimate, but uses them for GPU retention, not fetch timing.

What is defensible:
1. The measurement. On real SWE-agent traces, in a three-tier radix-tree engine, deciding tiers at arrival fails in both regimes, by different mechanisms.
   - Sparse regime: SSD reads are issued reactively, run one at a time on a single thread, and arrive in bursts. 58-80% of storage-hit TTFT is spent waiting behind other restores, while the SSD is about 75% idle.
   - Dense regime: the context matched at arrival is left unprotected. LRU plus FCFS evicts the head of the queue first, under write-through pressure that is itself mostly recompute. As a result 93-95% of prefill recomputes context that is still on the SSD, and the SSD tier contributes nothing.
   - In both regimes, inclusive mirroring costs about 40% of L2.
   - The same x70 load shows 59.5 s mean TTFT without SSD and 1.5-1.9 s with it, which suggests the regime is partly created by the cache policy itself.
2. One controller keyed on predicted admission time. It spans turns that have not yet arrived and turns already queued, and sets three things: the SSD fetch start (EDF, with a lead that accounts for the read backlog), the L2 protection horizon and budget, and the eviction order.
   - Relative to CachedAttention, this turns a window counted in jobs into a time horizon that also covers agent sessions still in their tool gap.
   - Relative to TokenCake and Ask the Tool, it extends the lead time to a contended SSD tier where fetches take seconds, and adds a queue-wait term.
   - None of the sources examined combines these.
3. A robustness study. Gap misprediction has an asymmetric cost: over-estimates only lose the gain, while under-estimates cost parking space and SSD re-reads. The fallback guarantees no regime does worse than today.

Honest framing: "forestall for agentic KV tiers", an incremental systems contribution. Its strength depends on two results:
- beating upstream's reactive re-query in the dense regime by a clear margin;
- keeping most of the oracle gain in the sparse regime with realistic, non-oracle gap prediction.

Two threats could shrink it:
- If the reactive admission re-query alone removes most dense-regime recompute, the remaining contribution is sparse-regime SSD timing. That is closest to TokenCake and Ask the Tool, and weaker.
- If reclaiming the mirror alone cuts x70 SSD returns from about 21% to 3-5%, as the LRU model predicts, the sparse-regime case also shrinks.
open_questions: Does a reactive admission-time L3 re-query alone break the x10/x1 recompute loop? Candidates are the upstream #40042 port and the local paced retry with tuned intervals. If it removes most of the recompute, the proactive part of Takeaway 2 saves only about 1 s of read time plus backlog per admission, which is small against a queue of about 100 s.

How predictable are real tool-return times, by tool type, in SWE-agent runs? These replays use deterministic trace gaps × scale. Session-history predictors fail on exactly the turns that end up on L3, because those have long gaps. Is a harness hint or live progress signal required?

How does the closed loop shift once recompute stops? Admission rate, queue depth and SSD read demand (37% of the SSD at today's rate) will all change. Device KV (668K tokens, about 24 contexts of 28K) may keep x1 queued even without recompute. At the same x70 load, the no-SSD arm averaged 59.5 s TTFT versus 1.5-1.9 s for the SSD arms, which suggests the regime depends partly on the cache policy.
Is the dense collapse bistable (metastable), or purely driven by capacity? The live set exceeds L1+L2 for 42-48% of the x10/x1 runs, so some L3 traffic is unavoidable even with perfect ordering.

Should protected content get soft eviction priority or a hard host lock? A hard lock can make write-through backups skip when evict_host cannot free enough space (unified_radix_cache.py:1412-1414). This has not happened so far (0 occurrences).

Does the nixl backend deduplicate h2s writes of recomputed pages, whose page hashes are identical? If not, about 0.6 GiB/s at x1 (57.97M tokens × 98,304 B over roughly 8,600 s) is spent rewriting pages L3 already holds.

How do the capacity lever and the timing lever combine at x70? The capacity lever reclaims the ~40% L2 mirror and demotes device evictions straight to L3. The LRU model predicts that reclaiming alone cuts SSD/cold returns from 21% to 2.7-4.5%.

Upstream semantics differ from this fork. Upstream (and HiRadixCache) keeps staged L3 pages pinned outside the tree until finalisation (#32724) and adds the admission re-query. The diagnosis, including the literal case where prefetched pages are evicted before use, must be re-checked after rebasing.
Would cache-aware admission remove the need for protection? This means admitting L2-resident requests first, as LPM or Strata-style deferral do. What would it cost in fairness and starvation?

Where does the regime switch lie between x70 and x10? There are no runs at x20-x50. How does the controller behave in the transition, where both early and late fetch are plausible and SSD reads compete with write-through?
With several instances, data parallelism, a shared L3 and a router, which instance serves the next turn (session affinity) changes the predicted admission time. How should the design handle that?
evaluation_plan: Step 0: fix the measurement before comparing anything. Pass aiohttp.TCPConnector(limit=0), or a limit of at least the session count, at replay_agentic.py:265 so that server arrival equals client send. Enable ReqTimeStats in every arm. Log per request: entry, admission, L3 enqueue/start/end, staged bytes, and protection start/end. Tag evict_host with the owning session where possible. Re-run baseline B0 at x70, x10 and x1, with at least 2-3 repetitions per arm (all current results are single runs).

Step 1: cheap falsification runs at x10/x1, which decide whether proactive timing is needed in the dense regime. (a) The local paced retry with interval ∈ {50, 500, 5,000} scheduling passes and a higher attempt cap. (b) Upstream's admission-time re-query, ported from #39283/#40042. (c) Queue-position eviction only (protect the queue head, evict the tail), with no fetch changes. Read out: recompute share, shared-prompt-only admission rate, host eviction rate, TTFT and admissions/s.

Step 2: oracle headroom. Give the design an oracle predicted admission time: the replay's known next arrival (end of reply + gap_slept) plus FCFS position with the measured admission rate. This bounds the benefit per regime. Proposed gate: if B3 (the reactive re-query) brings recompute below about 10% and is within about 10% of the oracle TTFT at x10/x1, drop proactive timing from the dense-regime claim.

Step 3: realistic prediction. Try four predictors: per-tool-type quantiles learned online (tool name taken from the generated tool call in the SWE-bench traces), session history, a harness-declared duration, and a progress-signal variant if the harness can emit one. Also re-run with stochastic gaps resampled from per-tool distributions, so the replay is not deterministic.

Workloads and regimes: gap scale x70, x40, x20, x10, x5 and x1 (to map where the regime switches); 64, 128 and 192 sessions; L2 of 80, 160 and 240 GB; SSD bandwidth at 1x and throttled to 0.5x; prefetch_threshold 256 vs 64.

Baselines: B0 arrival-time prefetch (three_tier_to, three_tier_wc). B1 hbm_host and hbm_lru. B2 local paced retry. B3 upstream reactive re-query. B4 CachedAttention look-ahead (prefetch window of Cmem/Skv jobs plus eviction exemption). B5 PCR (fixed 4-request window plus look-ahead LRU). B6 TokenCake / Ask-the-Tool style: refresh one transfer time before the predicted return, with no queue or backlog term and no protection. B7 write_back (non-inclusive L1/L2). B8 LPM cache-aware admission. B9 (optional) Cake-style compute-while-loading.

Metrics: returning-turn TTFT (mean, p50, p90, p99) by tier (device, host, SSD, recompute) and by regime; server wait (entry to admission) and client lag, reported separately; tokens recomputed after arrival and their share of prefill; shared-prompt-only admission rate; admissions/s and per-session makespan; SSD read and write GiB, utilization and read amplification (bytes read / bytes used); deadline misses (fetch finished after admission); staged and protected bytes and waste (evicted or unused before admission); host eviction rate; backup skips; GPU prefill time share.

Ablations: timing terms (read size only, + L3 backlog, + queue wait); EDF vs FIFO reads; protection off, soft priority or hard lock; horizon H ∈ {5, 10, 20, 30, 60 s} and budget β; eviction key LRU vs predicted admission; admission re-check on/off; quantile q ∈ {0.1, 0.25, 0.5}; mirror reclaim with L3-only demotion on/off.

Robustness: inject gap-prediction error e ∈ {−50, −25, 0, +25, +50}% plus heavy-tailed noise. Check that the worst case never falls below B0 (the fallback holds), and report SSD read amplification and staging waste.

Proposed success criteria. At x70: storage-hit TTFT p50 at or below about 0.5 s, and mean returning TTFT within about 15% of the oracle with realistic predictors. At x10/x1: recompute share below 10%, with better TTFT and admissions/s than B3. In every regime: no worse than B0, and SSD read amplification at or below about 1.2x.
headroom_estimates: x70 sparse regime, Takeaway 1 upper bound (oracle arrival, EDF, 20 s lead). Storage-hit TTFT mean 5.18 → 1.27 s (three_tier_to) and 5.57 → 0.32 s (three_tier_wc). A contention-free counterfactual gives 1.11 / 0.23 s. Mean returning TTFT 1.94 → 1.17 s (−40%) and 1.48 → 0.50 s (−66%). Addressable set: 19.7% / 18.6% of returning turns.

x70 with realistic leads. A 10 s lead hides 81-91% of fetch time (storage-hit TTFT mean 1.63 / 1.32 s). A lead of only the own read time hides 16-24%. Without protection, fetched content is re-evicted at 1% / 5-7% / 20-25% / 56-64% for leads of 10 / 20 / 30 / 60 s, and at 77% when fetching at the end of the reply. At 10-20 s leads, parked content averages 5-14% of L2 (peak 27%).

x70 limited by prediction. With a 2 s margin, a −25% gap error still nets 85-88% and −50% nets 55-63%. An over-estimate of 25% or more nets about 0-1%: it falls back to today's behaviour. Session-history predictors net 54-71% and add 500-700 GiB of extra SSD reads (against 1,571-1,810 GiB actually read).

x70 competing capacity lever. Reclaiming the roughly 40% of L2 that mirrors L1 (about 651K tokens, about 64 GB) would raise unique capacity from 1.64-1.66M to 2.30M tokens. A session-level LRU model predicts SSD/cold returns fall from 21.0% to 2.7-4.5%, which would shrink Takeaway 1's addressable set 4-8x. This is a model estimate, not a measurement.

x10/x1 dense regime, Takeaway 2 upper bound on work. 49.4-54.4M recomputed tokens are 93-95% of all prefill. 98.4-99.6% of these turns had their context in L1+L2 at arrival, and all of it was on SSD. At x1, new prefill per admitted turn would fall from about 20.7K tokens (7,490 tok/s ÷ 0.362 admissions/s) to about 1.0-1.1K. Write-through and SSD writes would fall from 54-58M tokens to roughly the x70 level of about 5M, so host eviction pressure (about 7K tok/s) would drop about 10x.

x10/x1 bandwidth. Reloading every admitted context just in time at x1 needs about 0.6-0.7 GiB/s, i.e. 32-37% of the 1.88 GiB/s SSD. Per-read throughput is 1.85-3.12 GiB/s at p50. Queue-aware eviction reduces this to the part of the queue that does not fit in L2 (queued private context 0.9-1.8M tokens vs at most 0.96M of host-only L2). Today's SSD write stream at x1 is about 0.6 GiB/s, mostly rewriting recomputed pages.

x10/x1 protection cost. A 10 s protection horizon at x1 holds about 0.362/s × 10 s × 20.6K ≈ 75K tokens, about 5% of L2. Pinning the whole queue would need about 1.59M tokens, roughly all of L2, which is infeasible.

x10/x1 TTFT cannot be estimated from these runs. The load is closed-loop, so recompute is both a symptom and a cause of the 100-110 s mean queue. At the same x70 load, hbm_host averaged 59.5 s TTFT against 1.5-1.9 s for the SSD arms, so recovering lost contexts can shift the operating point by an order of magnitude. x10/x1 still has to be measured. About 15% of x1 TTFT (19.9 s of 131.2 s) is client-side connection-cap lag, which no server change can remove.

The literal Takeaway 2 case, where prefetched L3 pages are evicted before admission, is small on its own. It wasted 0.91-0.94M (x10) and 0.21M (x1) SSD tokens that were read and discarded, 80-87% of real L3 reads. That is only 0.4-1.9% of lost tokens.

Inclusion at x10/x1. The total mirror is still about 39% of L2, but only 3-6.7% of L2 is idle mirror. The live set is at or above L1+L2 for 42-48% of the run. Reclaiming the mirror therefore helps much less in the dense regime than at x70.
